passage: For most of last year I was tired in a way sleep didn't touch. I went to bed early, drank water all day and was still thirsty, still dragging myself through the office. I told myself I was lazy and needed more discipline. I tried cold showers, a new planner, no screens at night. Nothing changed. My sister Shreya noticed me refilling my bottle again and again at her birthday lunch. "Sumit, this isn't willpower," she said. "Please see a doctor." I nearly laughed it off. But I went. The doctor listened, asked a lot of questions and ran some tests. It turned out there was a physical reason, and a plan to manage it. I'm less tired now. I wish I'd stopped guessing sooner.

qa.q: What did Shreya notice at her birthday lunch?
qa.a: Sumit refilling the bottle again and again.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel about the tiredness before seeing the doctor?
qa.a: Sumit felt frustrated and ashamed, blaming it on laziness and a lack of discipline.

qa.q: What was the wise choice, and why?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor instead of trying more tricks, because tiredness and thirst that rest and water do not fix can have a physical cause.

qa.q: How does Shreya see what is happening?
qa.a: She sees that it is not about willpower and is worried enough to ask Sumit plainly to see a doctor.

grounding: Shows someone whose fatigue and constant thirst continue despite rest and drinking choosing to see a doctor instead of blaming willpower.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Accounts team, filed privately.
For several weeks Deepika, usually one of our sharpest people, has seemed worn out. She yawns through morning meetings, keeps a large bottle on her desk and refills it often, and told me she has been sleeping long hours and drinking plenty yet still feels drained. Her work is still careful, but she looks exhausted. Today I asked her for a quiet word. I said I wasn't worried about her output, only about her. She admitted she had been blaming herself for being lazy. I said that when tiredness and thirst keep going despite rest, it is worth checking with a doctor rather than guessing. She agreed and booked an appointment. I have given her the morning off for it and will check in with her next week, only about how she is.
Sarita

qa.q: What did Deepika keep on her desk?
qa.a: A large bottle, which she refills often.

qa.q: How had Deepika been feeling about her tiredness?
qa.a: She felt drained and blamed herself for being lazy.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Sarita asked privately, focused on Deepika rather than her output, suggested a doctor and gave time off for the appointment, which made getting checked easy.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel after the talk?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and less ashamed, knowing her supervisor cared about her rather than just her work.

grounding: Illustrates tiredness and thirst that continue despite rest and drinking being checked by a doctor instead of pushed through with willpower.

passage:
Thursday, 10 pm
Something's off, and I've stopped pretending it isn't. For about a month I've been exhausted even after long nights of sleep. And thirsty, weirdly thirsty, finishing a whole bottle and still wanting more. I've tried everything I can think of: early nights, less screen, more water, fewer coffees. Nothing has changed.
Tonight Lalit found me asleep on the sofa at eight with my shoes on. He said, very gently, "Arohi, this isn't a willpower thing. Please get it checked." I wanted to argue that I'm just busy. But I've been saying that for a month.
So. Booked the clinic for Saturday morning. Writing down what I've noticed so I don't forget: tired, thirsty, up at night to pee, since roughly early June.
Scared, a bit. Also relieved I've stopped guessing.

qa.q: When is the clinic appointment?
qa.a: Saturday morning.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel after booking the clinic?
qa.a: Arohi feels a bit scared, but also relieved to have stopped guessing.

qa.q: Why is writing down the symptoms a sensible step?
qa.a: It gives the doctor a clear picture of what has been happening and since when, so nothing is forgotten in the appointment.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Arohi's tiredness?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as something to be checked rather than a willpower problem, and gently urges a visit to the doctor.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose tiredness and thirst continue despite rest and drinking, choosing to see a doctor rather than keep guessing.

passage: Imran taught Class 8 maths at the zilla parishad school in Wai, and for six weeks he had dragged himself through each day. He slept early. He drank from the matka in the staffroom so often the other teachers joked about it. Still he felt heavy, and still his mouth felt dry. He told himself it was the heat, then the new syllabus, then his age, though he was only twenty-five. One Sunday his friend Yogesh watched him doze off mid-sentence over tea at the stall. "Enough guessing, Imran. You rested, you drank. It's not working. We're going to the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow. I'll come on the bus with you." Imran opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. On Monday he took half a day's leave, and they caught the eight o'clock bus to Satara together.

qa.q: Where did Imran drink water at school?
qa.a: From the matka in the staffroom.

qa.q: Why did Imran keep blaming the heat and the syllabus?
qa.a: He felt worn down but reluctant to face that something might be wrong, so guessing felt easier than a check.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh right to push for the district hospital?
qa.a: Rest and water had not helped over weeks, so a doctor was needed to look for a physical cause that willpower can't fix.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt watching Imran doze off mid-sentence?
qa.a: Yogesh was likely worried and fed up with the guessing, which is why he offered to come on the bus.

grounding: Shows a young adult with weeks of tiredness and thirst despite rest and drinking being helped to see a doctor instead of guessing.

passage: For a month Anders had been dragging himself through his job at the Oslo shipping office. He drank water constantly and was still thirsty, went to bed early and still woke up exhausted. He tried cutting sugar, walking at lunch, sleeping more. Nothing changed. 'Maybe I'm just lazy,' he told his sister Olga over dinner. Olga put down her fork. 'Lazy people aren't thirsty all day. That's your body saying something. Book a doctor.' Anders hesitated; he hated fuss. But the next morning he called the clinic, got an appointment for Thursday, and wrote down everything he'd noticed so he wouldn't forget.

qa.q: When was Anders's appointment?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Anders hesitate before booking the doctor?
qa.a: He felt reluctant to make a fuss and half-believed he was just lazy.

qa.q: What made Anders's response a sensible one?
qa.a: When rest and small changes didn't help, he booked a doctor and wrote down what he'd noticed instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Olga see Anders's tiredness?
qa.a: Olga felt concerned and saw it as a body signal, not laziness, so she urged a doctor.

grounding: A young man with ongoing tiredness and thirst despite rest stops guessing and sees a doctor.
